title: History of India
description: India's history from the Harappan cities to the Republic: early kingdoms, the Mauryas and Guptas, southern dynasties, the Sultanates, Vijayanagara, the Mughals and Marathas, colonial rule, the freedom struggle, Partition and nation-building. Evidence-based, balanced across regions and communities, with interpretations and traditions clearly labelled.

lessons.title: Why We Celebrate 15 August
objectives: Explain that India became independent on 15 August 1947
Describe how we celebrate Independence Day
explanation: A long time ago — before your grandparents were born — India was ruled by the British. Many Indians wanted India to be free to rule itself.

After many years of struggle, India became independent on 15 August 1947. We celebrate this day every year as Independence Day, by hoisting the flag, singing the national anthem and remembering those who worked for freedom.
On 26 January we celebrate Republic Day, when India's Constitution started in 1950. There is a big parade in New Delhi.

context.text: India gained independence from British rule on 15 August 1947; the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.

At midnight we heard the news on the radio and people cried with joy. The next morning, flags were everywhere." Ivaan waved his little paper flag proudly.

lessons.title: Bapu and Friends
objectives: Name some people who worked for India's freedom
Know that Gandhi used peaceful ways
explanation: Mahatma Gandhi, called Bapu, led millions of people in peaceful protests against British rule. He believed in truth and non-violence (ahimsa). His birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday.

Many others worked for freedom: Jawaharlal Nehru became India's first Prime Minister; Sarojini Naidu was a poet and leader; Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army; Dr B. R. Ambedkar led the writing of the Constitution.
Millions of ordinary people — farmers, workers, students, women — also joined. Freedom was won by many hands.

context.text: Gandhi led major movements such as the Salt March (1930); Nehru served as Prime Minister from 1947 to 1964.

lessons.title: After the Battle of Kalinga
objectives: Retell the story of Ashoka after Kalinga
Know how we know about Ashoka (his edicts)
explanation: Ashoka was an emperor of the Mauryan Empire over 2,200 years ago. His empire covered most of the Indian subcontinent.

After conquering Kalinga (in present-day Odisha), Ashoka saw how many people had died or suffered. He felt deep regret and decided to rule by dhamma — kindness, honesty, respect for all people and care for animals.
We know this because Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and pillars — the edicts. The Lion Capital from one of his pillars, at Sarnath, is India's national emblem today.

context.text: Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII describes his remorse after the Kalinga war; his edicts are primary sources from the 3rd century BCE.
Historians discuss how fully Ashoka's ideals were put into practice across his empire.

story.title: The Emperor Who Changed
story.text: After the great battle of Kalinga, Ashoka walked across the battlefield. He saw families crying and fields ruined. "What have I done?" he thought. From then on, he sent messages carved on rocks across his empire: be kind, respect all beliefs, care for animals, plant trees by the roads.

lessons.title: Shivaji and the Forts of Maharashtra
objectives: Describe Shivaji Maharaj's achievements
Recognise that India's history includes many regions and rulers
explanation: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj (1630–1680) founded the Maratha kingdom in the 17th century. He built and captured hill forts like Raigad and Pratapgad, created a strong navy along the Konkan coast, and was crowned in 1674.
He is remembered in Maharashtra and beyond for courage, clever strategy and administration.
India has many great rulers from different regions: Raja Raja Chola built the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur; Akbar ruled the Mughal Empire; Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi fought the British in 1857.

context.text: Shivaji's coronation took place at Raigad in 1674; contemporary documents, letters and later chronicles record his reign.
Many popular stories about Shivaji are told in ballads (powadas); some details are traditional and historians compare them with documentary evidence.

lessons.title: Kingdoms of the Ganga Plain
objectives: Describe the Vedic period and the rise of kingdoms
Explain how we know about this period
explanation: After the Harappan cities declined, new societies developed in north India. The Vedas — collections of hymns in early Sanskrit — were composed and passed on orally for centuries; scholars date the earliest, the Rigveda, to roughly 1500–1200 BCE.
By around 600 BCE, sixteen large states called mahajanapadas arose, such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti, with towns, coins and armies.
This was also the time of the Buddha and Mahavira, whose teachings founded Buddhism and shaped Jainism. Magadha grew into the most powerful kingdom, the base of later empires.

context.text: Dating of the Vedas relies on linguistic and textual analysis; archaeological evidence from sites on the Ganga plain shows the growth of towns and punch-marked coins around the 6th century BCE.
For many Hindus, the Vedas are sacred and regarded as eternal revelation (shruti); historians study them as ancient texts.
Scholars continue to debate many aspects of the Vedic period, including dates and the movement of peoples.

vocabulary.meaning: an ancient collection of Sanskrit hymns and texts

story.title: The Memorising Students
story.text: For centuries, the Vedas were not written down. Students memorised every word, chanting with exact sounds and rhythms, checking each other in clever patterns. Scholars marvel that texts were passed on so accurately by memory alone — and UNESCO recognises Vedic chanting as intangible heritage.

lessons.title: Science and Art in the Gupta Period
objectives: Describe the Mauryan and Gupta empires
Explain achievements in science, mathematics and art
explanation: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 322 BCE; tradition links his adviser Kautilya (Chanakya) to the Arthashastra, a text on statecraft. Ashoka was his grandson.

The Gupta Empire (about 320–550 CE) saw remarkable achievements. Aryabhata (born 476 CE) wrote on astronomy and mathematics, proposing that the Earth rotates. Indian mathematicians developed the decimal place-value system with zero, later spread worldwide.

Kalidasa wrote famous Sanskrit plays and poems. Art flourished in temples and in the Ajanta caves, though Ajanta also includes earlier works. Some historians call this a "golden age", while others note it was golden mainly for elites.

context.text: Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya (499 CE) survives; the earliest clear use of zero as a number in a written rule appears in Brahmagupta's work (628 CE).
The label "golden age" is debated; historians point out that social inequalities persisted.

examples: India's first satellite was named Aryabhata.

lessons.title: Cholas, Sultans and Hampi
objectives: Describe the Chola, Delhi Sultanate and Vijayanagara states
Explain their achievements using evidence
explanation: The Cholas of Tamil Nadu (strongest about 850–1250 CE) built magnificent temples like the Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur and had a powerful navy that sailed to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

In north India, the Delhi Sultanate (from 1206) was ruled by several dynasties, including the Khaljis and Tughlaqs. It introduced new styles of architecture, like the Qutb Minar, and Persian became an important court language.
The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1565) in the south had a grand capital at Hampi, admired by foreign travellers for its markets and temples. It declined after the battle of Talikota (1565).

context.text: Chola inscriptions, temple records and foreign travellers' accounts (such as those of Domingo Paes and Abdur Razzaq for Vijayanagara) are key sources.
Historians debate the nature of religious and political relations in this period; sources reflect the perspectives of their authors.

lessons.title: Empires and Saints
objectives: Describe the Mughal and Maratha states
Explain the significance of Bhakti and Sufi movements
explanation: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in 1526 after the first battle of Panipat. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) built a strong administration, encouraged debates between scholars of different faiths, and is known for a policy often described as sulh-i-kul ("peace with all"). Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb expanded the empire to its largest extent, but his reign also saw conflict and revolts.
The Maratha state, founded by Shivaji, expanded in the 18th century under the Peshwas, becoming the most powerful force in much of India before the British rise.

Bhakti saints (like Kabir, Mirabai, Tukaram, Namdev and Guru Nanak, who founded Sikhism) and Sufi saints (like Nizamuddin Auliya) taught devotion and equality, often in local languages, attracting followers across communities.

context.text: The Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl documents Akbar's administration; Mughal and Maratha records, travellers' accounts and devotional poetry are key sources.
Assessments of rulers like Akbar and Aurangzeb differ among historians and are debated in public life; students should examine evidence and multiple views.
Sikhs revere Guru Nanak as the founder of their faith and the first of ten Gurus.

lessons.title: How the British Took Control
objectives: Explain how the East India Company gained power
Evaluate economic and social effects of colonial rule
explanation: European traders — Portuguese, Dutch, French and British — came for spices and textiles. The British East India Company, founded in 1600, built trading posts, then forts and armies.

After the Battle of Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), the Company controlled Bengal's revenues and expanded across India through wars and alliances. After the revolt of 1857, the British Crown took direct control in 1858.

Colonial rule brought railways, telegraphs and English education, but these served British interests. Indian handloom industries declined, wealth flowed to Britain ("drain of wealth", as Dadabhai Naoroji argued), and famines killed millions.

context.text: The Battle of Plassey (1757) and the 1858 Act transferring power to the Crown are well documented; major famines such as the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 and the 1943 Bengal famine caused millions of deaths.
Historians debate the economic impact of colonial rule in detail; Naoroji's "drain theory" was influential among nationalists and is still discussed.

lessons.title: Many Roads to Freedom
objectives: Describe key phases and leaders of the freedom movement
Compare different strategies for freedom
explanation: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Early leaders petitioned for reforms; later leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak demanded swaraj, and the Swadeshi movement (1905) boycotted British goods after the partition of Bengal.

Gandhi led mass non-violent movements: Non-Cooperation (1920–22), the Salt March and Civil Disobedience (1930), and Quit India (1942). Revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh chose different methods, and Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army.

Leaders like Dr B. R. Ambedkar fought for the rights of Dalits, insisting that freedom must include social equality. Women such as Sarojini Naidu, Aruna Asaf Ali and countless others played major roles. Independence came on 15 August 1947.

context.text: The Salt March from Sabarmati to Dandi (12 March–6 April 1930) and the Quit India resolution (8 August 1942) are well documented.
Historians debate the relative contribution of different movements, leaders and international factors to independence.

lessons.title: The Partition of 1947
objectives: Analyse causes and consequences of Partition
Use oral histories respectfully
explanation: Independence in 1947 came with the partition of British India into India and Pakistan (then including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh). Causes included growing communal tensions, political demands such as the Muslim League's call for Pakistan, and British policies and the rushed timeline of withdrawal.

Partition led to one of the largest migrations in history: around 12–15 million people crossed borders, and hundreds of thousands — estimates range up to about a million or more — were killed in violence. Many families lost homes and loved ones.

After independence, over 560 princely states were integrated into India, a process led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon. Partition's memories live on in families, literature and oral history archives.

context.text: Estimates of displacement (about 12–15 million) and deaths (from several hundred thousand to around a million or more) come from historians' analyses of census and other records; exact figures remain uncertain.
Historians in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Britain debate responsibility for Partition; students should study multiple perspectives with care and empathy.

lessons.title: Seventy-Five Years of a Republic
objectives: Describe major developments in independent India
Evaluate challenges and achievements
explanation: India adopted its Constitution in 1950 and held its first general elections in 1951–52 with universal adult franchise — a bold experiment in a largely poor and newly independent country.

States were reorganised along linguistic lines from 1956. Five-Year Plans built industry, dams and institutions like the IITs. The Green Revolution raised food production. The Emergency (1975–77), when civil liberties were suspended, tested democracy; it ended with elections in 1977.

Economic liberalisation in 1991 brought faster growth; India built space capability, IT industries and digital public infrastructure. Challenges remain: poverty, inequality, jobs, environmental pressures and social divisions. How to evaluate these decades is a matter of ongoing debate.

context.text: Key dates: Constitution (1950), first general elections (1951–52), States Reorganisation Act (1956), Emergency (June 1975–March 1977), economic reforms (1991).

story.title: The Great Experiment
story.text: In 1951, observers abroad doubted that a country with low literacy could run fair elections for 170 million voters. India printed symbols on ballots, trained hundreds of thousands of officials and set up polling stations in deserts and mountains. The election succeeded — and India has held regular elections ever since.
